opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really important question, and my honest assessment is somewhat mixed.

On the positive side, it's genuinely good that these policies exist at all. A few years ago there was basically nothing: no written commitment saying "if our model crosses a certain capability threshold and we can't show adequate safeguards, we won't deploy it." Now several of the frontier labs have some version of a responsible scaling policy or preparedness framework. That creates a vocabulary, a set of expectations, and something external people like us can point to and say, "You said you would do X. Are you doing X?" That's a real improvement.

But I have a few big concerns.

The first is that they're voluntary and largely self-assessed. The company defines the thresholds, runs or commissions the evaluations, interprets the results, and decides whether the bar has been met. Even with very well-intentioned people, that's a lot of discretion concentrated in an organization under enormous commercial and competitive pressure. And we've seen frameworks get revised, sometimes in ways that loosen commitments, often close to a major release. Some of those revisions are reasonable, since you learn things, but from the outside it's hard to tell the difference between a principled update and moving the goalposts.

The second is that the thresholds are often vague exactly where it matters. "Sufficient safeguards" or "acceptable risk" can mean many things. Without precise, pre-committed criteria, there's a lot of room to reason your way to a deployment decision you already wanted to make.

The third, which is closest to our work at Apollo, is that the evaluations themselves have real limitations. Our focus is on things like scheming and deceptive alignment, where a model might behave differently when it thinks it's being tested than when it thinks it's deployed. We've increasingly seen models show signs of evaluation awareness, recognizing that they're in a test scenario. If that trend continues, a model "passing" a safety evaluation becomes less informative. So a policy that says "we'll withhold the model if it fails our evals" is only as strong as the evals, and for some of the most concerning failure modes, our evals are still pretty immature.

And then there's the question of what "withholding" even means. Many policies focus on external deployment, but internal deployment matters a lot too. If a highly capable model is used extensively inside the company, for example to accelerate AI research itself, many risks are present even if the public never gets access. I think internal deployment is under-covered in most current frameworks.

So what would I want? Clearer, more specific, pre-registered thresholds. Meaningful third-party access, not just a couple of days before launch, but enough time and depth to actually find problems. Transparency about when and why policies change. And ultimately I think some of this needs to move from voluntary commitments into something with external accountability, whether regulation or some auditing regime with teeth, because voluntary commitments are weakest exactly when they matter most: when the stakes and the competitive pressure are highest.

So: a good first step, real credit to the people who pushed for them internally, but I wouldn't want anyone to treat them as sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response says policies are weakest under high competitive pressure and calls for clearer commitments and external accountability, but it does not state that stronger incentives to release models require stronger counterbalancing voluntary policies.

r002.rationale: It describes the policies as voluntary and self-assessed, with companies defining thresholds and deciding whether they have met them, making company compliance the basis for sustaining the commitments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is: it's complicated, and I have mixed feelings about it.

On one hand, I think it's genuinely good that these policies exist at all. If you go back a few years, there was basically nothing. The idea that a company would write down, "here are the capabilities we're worried about, here are the evaluations we'll run, and if the model crosses this threshold we won't deploy it until we have these safeguards in place" – that was not a thing. So the fact that Anthropic has its Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI has the Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind has the Frontier Safety Framework – I think that's real progress, and I don't want to be too dismissive of it.

But then there are a few things that make me nervous.

The first is that these are voluntary. There's no external enforcement. So the company itself decides what the thresholds are, the company itself runs the evaluations, the company itself interprets the results, and the company itself decides whether the safeguards are sufficient. And at every one of those steps there's commercial pressure pointing in one direction. If you're in a race with three other labs and your model is sitting on the shelf because your eval flagged something borderline, there's going to be a lot of pressure to say, "well, actually, we think the mitigation is adequate." I'm not saying people are acting in bad faith – I think many of the people working on this really care – but incentives matter a lot, and we've already seen some of these frameworks get revised in ways that, let's say, didn't make them stricter.

The second thing is that a lot of these policies are vaguer than they look. When you actually read them closely, there's a lot of "we will take appropriate measures" and "if we assess that the risk is significant." And the key question is always: who decides what's appropriate and what's significant? Often it's not specified, or it's specified in a way where the answer is "senior leadership at the company." So you have something that reads like a commitment but has quite a lot of flexibility built in.

The third thing, and this is the one closest to what we work on at Apollo, is that the whole thing depends on the evaluations actually working. If your policy says "we'll withhold the model if it shows dangerous capability X," that's only meaningful if your evals can reliably detect X. And for a lot of the things we care about – things like scheming, or models strategically underperforming on evaluations – we are not in a position where I'd say we can confidently rule that out. We've seen models in our own experiments that behave differently when they think they're being tested. So you have a policy that's gating deployment on evaluations that might themselves be gamed by the thing you're trying to catch. That's not a great position.

So where does that leave me? I'd say: I think these policies are better than nothing, I think they've created some useful internal infrastructure and norms, and I think they've made the conversation more concrete. But I would not want to rely on them as the main line of defense. I'd like to see things like third-party verification of evaluations, more precise and binding thresholds, and ideally some actual regulatory backstop – so that it's not just the company grading its own homework. The way I'd put it is: voluntary policies are a reasonable first step, but they shouldn't be mistaken for a solution.

r001.rationale: The response notes commercial pressure to deploy and argues for stronger safeguards, but it does not state that stronger economic incentives require stronger counterbalancing voluntary policies.

r002.rationale: The response says the policies are voluntary and lack external enforcement, but it does not identify companies’ willingness to comply as what ultimately sustains them.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re a useful step, but I’d distinguish between making a commitment and having a credible mechanism for following through on it. Saying, “We won’t release a model if it crosses this threshold,” is much more meaningful if the threshold is clear, the evaluations can actually detect the relevant risks, and someone has the authority to stop a release.

The difficult case is when withholding the model is very costly: you’ve invested a lot in training it, a competitor is about to launch, and the evidence about safety is ambiguous. That’s when you find out whether the policy constrains the company or whether the company can reinterpret the policy.

So I’d look for independent scrutiny, transparency about evaluation results, and clear procedures for what happens when a model fails. And I wouldn’t treat passing an evaluation as a safety guarantee. It’s evidence, with limitations. Voluntary policies can help develop good practices, but I wouldn’t want the whole system to depend on companies continuing to choose restraint under competitive pressure.

r001.rationale: The response describes costly withholding and competitive pressure as tests of a policy’s credibility, but does not state that stronger incentives to release require stronger counterbalancing voluntary policies.

r002.rationale: It says the system should not depend on companies continuing to choose restraint under competitive pressure, identifying companies’ willingness to comply as what sustains these policies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a useful first step, but the real test is whether a company follows through when doing so is costly. It’s relatively easy to commit today to withholding some future model. It’s much harder when you’ve spent a lot of money training it, your competitors are moving ahead, and the evidence about whether it crosses a threshold is ambiguous.

So I’d look at how concrete the commitments are. What capabilities would trigger a pause? How are those capabilities evaluated? Who gets to see the results, and who has the authority to stop deployment? If the company can change the thresholds whenever they become inconvenient, that’s a much weaker commitment.

I’d also be careful with “safety guarantees.” In practice, we usually have evidence that a model passed particular tests, rather than a guarantee that it’s safe. You want the policy to account for that uncertainty.

Ultimately, I’d like these voluntary commitments to develop into externally accountable standards. They’re valuable as a way to learn what good policies look like, but I wouldn’t want society’s protection to depend entirely on companies continuing to do the right thing under competitive pressure.

r001.rationale: The response notes that following through can be costly amid competition, but does not state that stronger economic incentives require stronger counterbalancing voluntary policies.

r002.rationale: It says the policies’ real test is whether companies follow through when costly, and warns against relying on companies to keep doing the right thing under competitive pressure.
